blocks.title: Greenhouse effect
blocks.md: Gases such as **water vapour, carbon dioxide (CO₂), methane (CH₄) and nitrous oxide (N₂O)** trap heat radiated from the Earth. This **natural** greenhouse effect keeps the planet warm enough for life. The **enhanced** greenhouse effect results from extra gases released by burning fossil fuels, clearing forests and some farming (rice paddies, livestock).

blocks.title: Impacts in Africa
blocks.md: Possible impacts vary by region: changing and less reliable rainfall, more frequent droughts and floods, heat stress, spread of some diseases, lower crop yields, pressure on water, rising sea level threatening coasts and deltas, and loss of biodiversity. Africa has contributed little to global emissions but is vulnerable because many people depend on rain-fed farming.

items.text: More greenhouse gases in the air
Rainfall changes, sea-level rise, extreme events

blocks.caption: From greenhouse gas emissions to climate impacts.
blocks.alt: Four boxes joined by arrows from emissions to extra heat trapped and to impacts.

blocks.title: Responses
blocks.md: **Mitigation** reduces emissions or removes carbon: renewable energy, efficient stoves, protecting forests, tree planting. **Adaptation** copes with change: drought-tolerant crops, water storage, early-warning systems, flood defences, diversifying livelihoods. International action includes the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (1992), the Kyoto Protocol (1997) and the Paris Agreement (2015).

blocks.title: Avoid these errors
blocks.md:
- The ozone hole is a different problem from global warming.
- Climate is long-term average conditions; weather is short-term.
- A single hot year or one storm does not prove climate change.
- Mitigation and adaptation are not the same thing.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Classify
blocks.statement: Classify each as mitigation or adaptation: (a) planting forest, (b) building raised houses on a flood-prone coast, (c) installing solar panels.
steps: (b) Raised houses cope with flooding: adaptation.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Explain a link
blocks.statement: Explain how deforestation contributes to climate change.
steps: Trees store carbon as they grow.
Burning or rotting released CO₂ to the air.
Fewer trees remain to absorb CO₂, so more stays in the atmosphere and enhances warming.
blocks.answer: It releases stored carbon and removes a carbon sink.

blocks.title: Desertification
blocks.md: **Desertification** is land degradation in dry areas caused by climatic variation and human activity, turning productive land into desert-like conditions. It is not simply the spread of existing deserts. It is a concern in the **Sahel**, the semi-arid belt south of the Sahara, including the far north of Cameroon.

blocks.title: Causes and effects
blocks.md: **Causes:** recurring drought, overgrazing, over-cultivation without fallow, cutting wood for fuel, poor irrigation (salinisation) and population pressure. **Effects:** lower soil fertility and crop yields, loss of pasture, wind and water erosion, food shortages, migration and competition for resources.

blocks.caption: A chain of causes and effects in desertification.
blocks.alt: Four boxes connected by arrows from drought and population growth to falling yields and migration.

blocks.title: Lake Chad
blocks.md: Lake Chad is shared by Cameroon, Chad, Niger and Nigeria. Since the 1960s it has shrunk greatly because of lower rainfall and increased abstraction of water for irrigation and population needs, though it varies year to year. Fishing, farming and herding around the lake, and many people’s livelihoods, are affected. The Lake Chad Basin Commission (created in 1964) coordinates the neighbouring countries.

blocks.title: Management
blocks.md: Tree planting and shelterbelts, agroforestry, **zaï** pits and stone lines to hold water, improved cooking stoves, rotational grazing, small-scale irrigation, community land management, and regional projects such as the African Union’s **Great Green Wall** (launched in 2007). Success depends on local participation and secure land rights.

blocks.title: Common errors
blocks.md:
- Deserts do not simply ‘advance’ like a wave: degradation is local and caused by land use as well as climate.
- Drought is a natural event; desertification needs human pressure too.
- Do not give a precise area for Lake Chad without a source.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Explain overgrazing
blocks.statement: Explain how overgrazing contributes to desertification.
steps: Too many animals eat the grass faster than it regrows.
Hooves compact the soil and bare ground is exposed.
Wind and rain erode the topsoil.
Soil fertility and water retention fall, so less grass can grow.
blocks.answer: A cycle of vegetation loss, erosion and falling fertility.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Lake Chad impacts
blocks.statement: Give two likely consequences for people when Lake Chad shrinks.
steps: Fishing yields and fishing communities decline.
Fertile recession farmland and pasture shift or reduce.
Communities may migrate or compete for water and land.

blocks.title: Deforestation
blocks.md: **Deforestation** is the permanent clearing of forest for other uses. In central Africa the main direct causes are **agricultural expansion** (shifting cultivation and plantations), **logging**, **fuelwood and charcoal**, road building, mining and urban growth. Underlying causes include population growth, poverty, demand for timber and weak enforcement.

blocks.title: Consequences
blocks.md: **Environmental:** soil erosion and flooding, loss of habitat and biodiversity, disturbed water cycle and local climate, release of stored carbon. **Social and economic:** loss of forest products (bushmeat, medicines, fruits, honey), loss of land for forest communities, but also short-term income from timber and farming.

items.text: Clearing for farms, logging, fuelwood, roads
Soil erosion, lost habitats, less carbon storage

blocks.caption: From clearing to conservation.
blocks.alt: Four boxes: causes of clearing, falling forest cover, consequences, and conservation responses.

blocks.title: Cameroon and the Congo Basin
blocks.md: Cameroon’s southern and eastern forests belong to the Congo Basin, one of the largest tropical rainforests in the world. Protected areas include national parks and reserves such as Korup and Dja. Strategies: sustainable and certified logging, protected areas, **community forestry**, agroforestry, reforestation, efficient stoves and international schemes that pay to keep forests standing.

blocks.title: Avoid these errors
blocks.md:
- Logging is selective in many places; not all logging means total clearing.
- Protected areas fail without involving local people and enforcement.
- Planting a few trees does not replace the biodiversity of old forest.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Impact chain
blocks.statement: Explain how clearing forest on a steep slope can cause flooding downstream.
steps: Fewer trees mean less interception and less water taken up.
Bare soil allows rapid run-off and erosion.
Rivers receive water and sediment quickly and their channels silt up, so floods are more likely.
blocks.answer: Faster run-off and silted channels increase flood risk.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Conservation conflict
blocks.statement: A national park restricts hunting and farming at its boundary. Suggest how conflict with villagers could be reduced.
steps: Involve communities in planning and management.
Share benefits: jobs as guides, tourism revenue sharing.
Support alternative livelihoods and agroforestry near the boundary.
blocks.answer: Participation, benefit sharing and alternative livelihoods.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: Assess the effectiveness of mitigation and adaptation as responses to climate change in a developing country.
exercises.model: Mitigation, like renewable energy and forest protection, helps in the long term only if all major emitters act; one country’s effect is small. Adaptation gives immediate protection, for example by improving water storage and drought-tolerant seeds, but it can be costly and does not remove the cause. Best results combine both, with funding and technology transfer.

exercises.prompt: Evaluate the effectiveness of protected areas and community forestry as ways of conserving tropical forests.
exercises.model: Protected areas safeguard biodiversity and clear boundaries, but need funds, patrols and the acceptance of nearby people; they can restrict local livelihoods.
